To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the phonetic renderi ng of Cyrillic Roman and Chinese Pinyin transcriptions is not as accurate as it should be and that the phonetic alphabet is not the best way to represent the actual pronunciation of these languages.

(i) the phonetic alphabet is not always a reliable tool for representing the actual pronunciation; (ii) the phonetic transcription of the Cyrillic alphabet for Russian is not always accurate, especially for non native speakers; (iii) the same applies to the Pinyin phonetic transcription of Chinese; (iv) the mismatch between the actual pronunciation and the phonetic transcription may cause misinterpretations and misunderstandings in L2 or FL teaching and learning.
the phonetic transcription systems of Russian and Chinese are not always accurate, but they are still useful tools in the learning and teaching of the languages.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the phonetic renderin gs of the Cyrillic script for Russian and Pinyin for Modern Standard Chinese.
the phonetic renderi ngs of Russian and Mandarin Chinese, and the way these are taught and learned.
the analysis of the romanisations of both Russian and Chinese in order to improve the teaching and learning of these languages as foreign or second languages.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the transliterations of Cyrillic and Pinyin are far from being perfect.
the Roman alphabet is not suitable for transliterating Russian Cyrillic and Chinese Pinyin.

transliterations and transcriptions from Cyrillic to the Roman alphabet and vice versa and from Pinyin to the Roman alphabet should be as close as possible to their original phonetic rendering in order to prevent any kind of phonetic mismatching.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the phonetic alphabet has been designed to represent the sounds in the language.

the transliteration of Russian and of Mandarin Chinese into the Latin alphabet is not an easy task, and that the phonetic render ing and the pronunciation accuracy of the Cyrillic Roman alphabet and of Pinyin are not as simple and straightforward as it may seem at first.

, in the case of Chinese, the phonetic script Pinyin, as it is currently used, is not a phonetic alphabet in the strict sense, but a phonetic transcription, which, in the case at hand, is not always accurate.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the transliteration of the Cyrillic and Pinyin systems should be done in a way that reflects the pronunciation of the original languages, so that L2 students can learn to pronounce the target languages correctly and avoid mispronunciations that could lead to misunderstandings.
a phonetic transcription is not a phonetic transcription if it does not accurately reflect the phonetic reality.
, as a consequence of a phonetic alphabet being used, a transliteration is bound to be a misinterpretation, as the phonetics of a language is a highly dynamic and changing entity.
